topics.name: Executive branch
topics.kicker: Branch that carries out the laws · Led by the president under Article II
topics.briefing: Congress writes the nation’s laws, but the executive branch carries them out. Article II of the Constitution puts the president in charge of it and makes the president commander in chief; the president can also veto bills, make treaties with the Senate’s approval, grant pardons, and issue executive orders. The vice president, the 15 departments whose heads make up most of the Cabinet, and agencies from NASA to the FBI all belong to it.
topics.answerHtml: Executive branch (accept the executive; prompt on the president or presidency; do not accept “legislative branch,” “judicial branch,” or “Cabinet”)
accept: executive branch of the united states
executive branch of the federal government

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In _Federalist_ No. 70, Alexander Hamilton argued that “energy” in this branch is “a leading character in the definition of good government.” He added that this branch works best when one person leads it, a quality he called “unity.”
tossups.r: Article II of the Constitution created this branch. For 10 points, name this branch of government headed by the president.

tossups.p: A 1937 report by the Brownlow Committee declared that “the President needs help.” Two years later, Franklin Roosevelt created a new office of advisers for the leader of this branch and moved the Bureau of the Budget into it.
tossups.r: That bureau later became the Office of Management and Budget. For 10 points, name this branch of government that carries out the laws.

tossups.p: In _United States v. Nixon_, the Supreme Court ruled that a special privilege claimed by this branch could not be used to withhold the Watergate tapes from a criminal trial. That privilege lets officials of this branch keep some of their private advice secret.
tossups.r: Richard Nixon resigned as its leader soon after that 1974 ruling. For 10 points, name this branch of government headed by the president.

tossups.p: In _Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer_, the Supreme Court ruled that the head of this branch could not seize the nation’s steel mills without approval from Congress. Justice Robert Jackson’s opinion in that 1952 case explained when the powers of this branch are strongest and weakest.
tossups.r: The steel seizure was ordered by Harry Truman. For 10 points, name this branch of government led by the president.

tossups.p: In 1948, Harry Truman used a numbered directive to order an end to segregation in the armed forces, the kind of order the head of this branch can issue without a vote of Congress. Franklin Roosevelt’s 1942 order of that kind led to the forced removal of Japanese Americans to incarceration camps.
tossups.r: This branch carries out the laws that Congress passes. For 10 points, name this branch led by the president.

tossups.p: After a disappointed office seeker assassinated President James Garfield, the Pendleton Act of 1883 required that many jobs in this branch be filled through merit exams instead of being handed out as political rewards. That law weakened the “spoils system” associated with Andrew Jackson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of the U.S. government, which includes the president and the federal departments.

tossups.p: Passed over Richard Nixon’s veto in 1973, the War Powers Resolution requires the head of this branch to notify Congress within 48 hours of sending troops into combat, and it limits how long those troops can stay without Congress’s approval.
tossups.r: The head of this branch is commander in chief of the armed forces. For 10 points, name this branch of government.

tossups.p: In _Clinton v. City of New York_, the Supreme Court struck down a 1996 law that let the head of this branch cancel individual spending items in a bill after signing it. The Court ruled that this line-item veto broke the Constitution’s rules for how bills become laws.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of government whose leader can veto bills passed by Congress.

tossups.p: The Constitution gives the head of this branch the power to grant “Reprieves and Pardons” for federal crimes, except in cases of impeachment. In 1974, Gerald Ford used that power to pardon Richard Nixon for any federal crimes he might have committed as president.
tossups.r: Ford had taken over this branch’s top job when Nixon resigned. For 10 points, name this branch of government that carries out the laws.

tossups.p: The Articles of Confederation created no separate branch of this kind, so no single leader was in charge of carrying out the national government’s laws. At the Constitutional Convention, delegates argued over whether this branch should be led by one person or by a council of several people.
tossups.r: They chose one person, the president. For 10 points, name this branch created by Article II.

tossups.p: In _The Spirit of the Laws_, Montesquieu [“MON-tes-kyoo”] warned that liberty is lost if the power of this branch is joined with the power to make laws or the power to judge. The framers of the Constitution borrowed that idea, the separation of powers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of government, which enforces the laws and is led by the president.

tossups.p: Historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr. warned in a 1973 book that the leader of this branch had gained so much power, especially over war, that the office had become an “imperial presidency.” Schlesinger had earlier worked as a special assistant in John F. Kennedy’s White House.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of government created by Article II of the Constitution.

tossups.p: If the head of this branch holds a bill unsigned for ten days while Congress has adjourned, the bill dies in a “pocket veto.” Congress can override a regular veto from the head of this branch by a two-thirds vote in both houses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of government, which shares power with the legislative and judicial branches.

tossups.p: The Constitution says that the leader of this branch must be a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, and a resident of the United States for at least 14 years. That leader swears to “preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States.”
tossups.r: The vice president also belongs to this branch. For 10 points, name this branch of government led by the president.

tossups.p: The newest of the 15 departments in this branch, the Department of Homeland Security, was created in 2002 after the September 11 attacks. Its oldest departments, including State and Treasury, date from 1789.
tossups.r: The heads of those departments make up most of the Cabinet. For 10 points, name this branch of the U.S. government, whose leader is the president.

trap.title: Branch, group, or office?
trap.body: Several answer lines live inside this branch: the president, the vice president, the Cabinet, the Executive Office of the President (created in 1939), and single departments such as State or Defense. If a question asks for “this branch,” say “executive branch,” but if it asks for “this group of advisers,” the answer is the Cabinet. Executive orders, vetoes, and executive privilege are powers of this branch, not the branch itself.
trap.fix: Count the articles: Article I is the legislative branch (Congress makes the laws), Article II is the executive branch (the president carries them out), and Article III is the judicial branch (the courts interpret them). Saying only “the president” may earn a prompt, so add “executive branch.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Executive branch (accept the executive; prompt on the president or presidency; do not accept “legislative branch,” “judicial branch,” or “Cabinet”)

topics.name: Fourteen Points
topics.kicker: Woodrow Wilson’s plan for peace · Its last point called for a League of Nations
topics.briefing: On January 8, 1918, with World War I still being fought, President Woodrow Wilson told Congress his plan for a fair and lasting peace in fourteen numbered points. He called for an end to secret treaties, freedom of the seas, lower trade barriers, smaller armies, borders drawn along lines of nationality, and, in the last point, a League of Nations. Germany asked for peace on these terms, but the Treaty of Versailles left out many of them, and the U.S. Senate rejected that treaty.
topics.answerHtml: Fourteen Points (accept 14 Points; prompt on Points alone; do not accept “League of Nations” or “Treaty of Versailles”)
reject: covenant of the league of nations

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Colonel Edward House’s team of experts, known as “The Inquiry,” helped prepare this program, and the journalist Walter Lippmann helped draft it. Its author hoped it would answer the Bolsheviks [“BOHL-shuh-viks”], who had embarrassed the Allies by publishing their secret treaties.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 1918 plan for peace after World War I, presented by Woodrow Wilson.

tossups.p: Before the Allies accepted these proposals as the basis for an armistice, Britain rejected their call for “freedom of the seas,” and the Allies added that Germany must pay for damage done to civilians. Germany’s new chancellor, Prince Max of Baden, had asked for peace on these terms in October 1918.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this peace program that Woodrow Wilson announced to Congress in January 1918.

tossups.p: The thirteenth item of this program called for an independent Polish state with “free and secure access to the sea.” That demand led the peacemakers at Paris to give Poland a strip of land called the Polish Corridor, which cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany.
tossups.r: Its last item called for a League of Nations. For 10 points, name this January 1918 peace plan of Woodrow Wilson.

tossups.p: This program demanded that Belgium be evacuated and restored, that all French territory be freed, and that “the wrong done to France by Prussia in 1871” over Alsace-Lorraine be righted. It also called for Romania, Serbia, and Montenegro to be evacuated.
tossups.r: The Treaty of Versailles later returned Alsace-Lorraine to France. For 10 points, name this list of war aims announced by Woodrow Wilson in January 1918.

tossups.p: The first item of this program called for “open covenants of peace, openly arrived at,” so that diplomacy would “proceed always frankly and in the public view.” Its second item called for “absolute freedom of navigation upon the seas.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of proposals that Woodrow Wilson made for ending World War I.

tossups.p: Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, who chaired the Foreign Relations Committee, demanded changes called “reservations” before he would accept a treaty that was partly based on this program. The Senate rejected that treaty in 1919 and again in 1920.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this peace plan by Woodrow Wilson whose last item called for a League of Nations.

tossups.p: William Borah and other senators nicknamed the “Irreconcilables” opposed in any form the organization called for in the last item of this program. Many senators feared that Article X of that organization’s Covenant could drag the United States into foreign wars.
tossups.r: That organization was the League of Nations. For 10 points, name this plan for peace presented by Woodrow Wilson in 1918.

tossups.p: This program called for the Dardanelles [“dar-duh-NELZ”] to be permanently opened as a free passage for the ships of all nations. It also promised that the non-Turkish peoples of the Ottoman Empire would have the chance for “autonomous development.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this list of peace terms that Woodrow Wilson gave Congress in January 1918.

tossups.p: This program said that the peoples of Austria-Hungary should have “the freest opportunity to autonomous development,” and it called for Serbia to be given access to the sea. After the war, new countries such as Czechoslovakia formed from Austria-Hungary’s lands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan for peace, built on the idea of self-determination, that Woodrow Wilson announced in 1918.

tossups.p: One item of this program said that Italy’s borders should be redrawn “along clearly recognizable lines of nationality.” At the Paris Peace Conference, Italy’s Vittorio Orlando walked out for a time when Woodrow Wilson refused to give Italy the port of Fiume [“fee-OO-may”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan for peace that Wilson had announced to Congress during World War I.

tossups.p: While Russia’s new Bolshevik government was negotiating with Germany at Brest-Litovsk [“BREST lih-TOFSK”], this program called for all Russian territory to be evacuated. It also promised Russia “a sincere welcome into the society of free nations under institutions of her own choosing.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this peace program that Woodrow Wilson presented to Congress in January 1918.

tossups.p: This program called for an “impartial adjustment of all colonial claims,” in which the interests of the colonized peoples would have “equal weight” with the claims of governments. It also called for national armaments to be reduced as far as domestic safety allows.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan for peace whose last item called for a League of Nations.

tossups.p: Almost a year before giving this speech, its author had told the Senate that the world needed a “peace without victory.” He gave this speech about nine months after the United States entered World War I, in an address to a joint session of Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 1918 speech by Woodrow Wilson that listed his goals for peace.

tossups.p: This program’s author won the Nobel Peace Prize for 1919, mostly for his work creating the organization proposed in its final item. That item called for “a general association of nations” to protect the independence of “great and small states alike.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plan for peace presented by Woodrow Wilson in January 1918.

tossups.p: At the Paris Peace Conference, French premier Georges Clemenceau [“KLEM-un-soh”] demanded harsher terms for Germany than this program had promised, including large reparations payments. Clemenceau, Britain’s David Lloyd George, and Italy’s Vittorio Orlando joined this program’s author as the “Big Four.”
tossups.r: The Treaty of Versailles left out many of this program’s ideas. For 10 points, name this peace plan announced by Woodrow Wilson in January 1918.

trap.title: Speech, treaty, or league?
trap.body: Three answer lines share Woodrow Wilson, Henry Cabot Lodge, and the Senate fight of 1919–1920. The Fourteen Points were Wilson’s January 1918 speech listing his goals for peace; the League of Nations was the organization his last point called for; and the Treaty of Versailles was the 1919 peace treaty with Germany that created the League. Answering “League of Nations” or “Versailles” here is wrong, and so is mixing it up with the Fourteenth Amendment.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This speech,” “this plan,” or “these proposals,” with numbered items such as freedom of the seas or an independent Poland, means the Fourteen Points. “This organization,” Geneva, or Article X means the League; “this treaty,” the war guilt clause, or the Hall of Mirrors means Versailles.
trap.line: Real answer line: Fourteen Points (accept 14 Points; prompt on Points alone; do not accept “League of Nations” or “Treaty of Versailles”)

topics.name: Free Soil Party
topics.kicker: Antislavery third party · Fought the spread of slavery into the West
topics.briefing: In 1848, antislavery Democrats, Whigs, and Liberty Party members met in Buffalo, New York, and formed the Free Soil Party, whose slogan was “Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men.” The party did not call for ending slavery in the South, but it fought to keep slavery out of the western territories. Its candidate, former president Martin Van Buren, won no states, and from 1854 on, most Free Soilers joined the new Republican Party.
topics.answerHtml: Free Soil Party (accept Free Soilers; do not accept “Liberty Party” or “Republican Party”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This party was founded at an August 1848 convention in Buffalo, New York, which brought together New York’s “Barnburner” Democrats, Massachusetts’s “Conscience Whigs,” and most members of the Liberty Party, an earlier abolitionist party.
tossups.r: It opposed the spread of slavery into the western territories. For 10 points, name this third party that nominated Martin Van Buren for president in 1848.

tossups.p: Charles Francis Adams, the son of John Quincy Adams, was this party’s candidate for vice president in 1848. That year, its presidential candidate split the Democratic vote in New York, which helped the Whig Zachary Taylor win the election.
tossups.r: That candidate was former president Martin Van Buren. For 10 points, name this party that opposed spreading slavery to the West.

tossups.p: Senator John P. Hale of New Hampshire was this party’s candidate for president in 1852, with George Washington Julian of Indiana as his running mate. They won only about 5 percent of the popular vote.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antislavery party whose 1848 candidate had been Martin Van Buren.

tossups.p: This party grew out of support for a failed 1846 proposal by Pennsylvania congressman David Wilmot to ban slavery in any land the United States won from Mexico. That proposal passed the House more than once but died in the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this party, formed in 1848, that fought to keep slavery out of the western territories.

tossups.p: In 1849, Ohio’s legislature elected Salmon P. Chase to the U.S. Senate with the help of this party’s members, who had made a deal with the Democrats. Chase later served as Abraham Lincoln’s Secretary of the Treasury.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antislavery party that ran Martin Van Buren for president in 1848.

tossups.p: In 1851, a coalition of Democrats and members of this party in the Massachusetts legislature elected Charles Sumner to the U.S. Senate. Five years later, Sumner was attacked with a cane on the Senate floor by South Carolina congressman Preston Brooks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antislavery party of the late 1840s and early 1850s, whose members later joined the Republicans.

tossups.p: This party ran its last presidential campaign in 1852. Two years later, after the Kansas–Nebraska Act threatened to open new territories to slavery, most of its members joined antislavery Whigs and Democrats in forming a new party.
tossups.r: That new party was the Republican Party. For 10 points, name this antislavery party whose first presidential candidate was Martin Van Buren.

tossups.p: This party drew many New York Democrats nicknamed “Barnburners,” after a story about a farmer who burned down his own barn to get rid of the rats. Their rivals in New York’s Democratic Party were called “Hunkers.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this third party that nominated former president Martin Van Buren in 1848.

tossups.p: Most members of the Liberty Party, which had nominated James G. Birney for president in 1840 and 1844, joined this party in 1848. Unlike the Liberty Party, this party did not call for ending slavery where it already existed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this party that opposed the spread of slavery into the western territories.

tossups.p: Historian Eric Foner took most of this party’s slogan for the title of his 1970 book about the ideas of the early Republican Party. That four-part slogan began with this party’s own name and went on to promise “Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antislavery party that ran Martin Van Buren for president in 1848.

tossups.p: In 1848, this party won about 10 percent of the national popular vote but no electoral votes. Its presidential candidate finished ahead of the Democratic nominee, Lewis Cass, in New York, which helped Zachary Taylor carry that state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this third party whose candidate that year was former president Martin Van Buren.

tossups.p: Antislavery Whigs from Massachusetts, nicknamed “Conscience Whigs,” left their party to help form this one after the Whigs nominated Zachary Taylor, a slaveholding general. Their opponents in the Whig Party were called “Cotton Whigs.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antislavery party founded in 1848, whose first presidential candidate was Martin Van Buren.

tossups.p: Many members of this party wanted western lands saved for free white farmers and workers. The party also called for free land for western settlers, an idea later carried out by the Homestead Act.
tossups.r: Its first candidate was Martin Van Buren. For 10 points, name this antislavery third party of 1848 to 1854.

tossups.p: This party’s first presidential candidate had been elected president in 1836 as a Democrat and lost reelection to William Henry Harrison in 1840. That candidate came out of retirement to run again in 1848 as this party’s nominee.
tossups.r: That candidate was Martin Van Buren. For 10 points, name this third party formed in 1848.

tossups.p: The 1848 platform of this party answered Southern demands with the words “no more Slave States and no more Slave Territory.” Two years later, senators allied with it, such as Salmon Chase of Ohio, spoke out against the Compromise of 1850.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antislavery third party that nominated Martin Van Buren in 1848.

trap.title: Liberty, Free Soil, or Republican?
trap.body: Three antislavery parties came one after another. The Liberty Party ran the abolitionist James G. Birney in 1840 and 1844; the Free Soil Party ran Martin Van Buren in 1848 and John P. Hale in 1852 to stop slavery’s spread west; and the Republican Party, founded in 1854, took in most Free Soilers and elected Abraham Lincoln in 1860. Their clues overlap because many of the same people moved from one party to the next.
trap.fix: Birney and the early 1840s mean the Liberty Party. Van Buren, Charles Francis Adams, Hale, the Buffalo convention, and the slogan “Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men” mean the Free Soil Party. The Kansas–Nebraska Act, Ripon, Frémont, and Lincoln mean the Republicans. Kansas “Free-Staters” were antislavery settlers in Kansas, not this party.
trap.line: Real answer line: Free Soil Party (accept Free Soilers; do not accept “Liberty Party” or “Republican Party”)

topics.name: Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
topics.kicker: Part of the Compromise of 1850 · Forced free states to return freedom seekers
topics.briefing: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, part of the Compromise of 1850, made officials and even ordinary citizens in the free states help capture people who had escaped slavery. Accused people could not testify or have a jury trial, and a federal commissioner earned $10 for sending someone south but only $5 for setting someone free. The law turned many Northerners against slavery, drove thousands of Black Americans to Canada, and helped inspire _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_.
topics.answerHtml: Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 (accept Fugitive Slave Law; do not accept “Compromise of 1850” or “Kansas–Nebraska Act”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Senator James Mason of Virginia wrote this law, which paid federal commissioners ten dollars when they sent an accused person south but only five dollars when they set the person free. Critics said that difference was a bribe.
tossups.r: It passed as part of the Compromise of 1850. For 10 points, name this law that forced Northerners to help return people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: Southern leaders demanded this law after the Supreme Court ruled in _Prigg v. Pennsylvania_ that state officials did not have to help capture people who had escaped slavery. Several Northern states had then passed “personal liberty laws” that barred their officials and jails from helping.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1850 law that made it a federal job to return freedom seekers to their enslavers.

tossups.p: In February 1851, a group of Black abolitionists including Lewis Hayden rushed into a Boston courtroom and freed Shadrach Minkins, a waiter who had been arrested under this law. They helped Minkins escape to Canada.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, part of the Compromise of 1850, that required the return of people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: In 1854, President Franklin Pierce sent federal troops to Boston to make sure that Anthony Burns was returned to slavery in Virginia under this law. Thousands of protesters lined the streets as soldiers marched Burns to a ship.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law passed in 1850 to force the return of people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote in his journal that this law was a “filthy enactment” that he would not obey. In 1854, Henry David Thoreau attacked it in a Fourth of July speech called “Slavery in Massachusetts.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that required Northerners to help capture people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: A novel first published in installments in the antislavery newspaper _The National Era_ was written partly in response to this law. In that novel, the enslaved mother Eliza escapes with her young son by crossing the icy Ohio River.
tossups.r: That novel was Harriet Beecher Stowe’s _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_. For 10 points, name this law passed as part of the Compromise of 1850.

tossups.p: In _Ableman v. Booth_, the Supreme Court ruled that Wisconsin could not overrule this law, after newspaper editor Sherman Booth helped free Joshua Glover from a jail in Milwaukee. Wisconsin’s own supreme court had declared this law unconstitutional.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1850 law that required free states to return people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: Under this law, a person accused of escaping slavery was denied a jury trial and was not allowed to testify in his or her own defense. A sworn statement from the person claiming ownership was enough to send the accused south.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law signed by Millard Fillmore as part of the Compromise of 1850.

tossups.p: This law threatened anyone who helped a person escape slavery with a fine of up to $1,000 and six months in jail. It also let federal marshals order ordinary citizens to help catch people who had escaped.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1850 law that led many freedom seekers to flee all the way to Canada.

tossups.p: Stephen Douglas helped steer this law through Congress as one of several separate bills, after Henry Clay’s “Omnibus Bill” fell apart in the summer of 1850. It became law about two months after Zachary Taylor’s death.
tossups.r: Millard Fillmore signed it in September 1850. For 10 points, name this law about people who had escaped slavery, part of the Compromise of 1850.

tossups.p: William and Ellen Craft had escaped from Georgia in 1848, with Ellen disguised as a white man and William posing as her servant. Two years later, they fled from Boston to England after slave catchers came to seize them under this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that forced free states to help return people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: In the Jerry Rescue of 1851, abolitionists in Syracuse, New York, broke into the building where William Henry was being held under this law and helped him reach Canada. The rescue happened while the Liberty Party was meeting in the city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1850 law that required the return of people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: Early in the Civil War, General Benjamin Butler refused to return three men who had escaped to Fort Monroe, calling them “contraband of war” instead of following this law. Congress finally repealed this law in June 1864.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law from 1850 that required Northerners to help return people who had escaped slavery.

tossups.p: In 1860, Harriet Tubman helped a crowd in Troy, New York, free Charles Nalle, who was about to be sent back south under this law. Nine years earlier, federal officials in Boston had sent Thomas Sims back to slavery in Georgia under it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, part of the Compromise of 1850, that forced free states to return freedom seekers.

tossups.p: John Greenleaf Whittier’s poem “Ichabod” attacked Daniel Webster for supporting this law in his Seventh of March speech. In that speech, Webster said he spoke “not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that required the return of people who had escaped slavery, passed in 1850.

clues.t: Part of the Compromise of 1850, proposed by Henry Clay
Required officials and citizens in the free states to help return people who had escaped slavery
Drove many freedom seekers and free Black Americans to flee to Canada; the Underground Railroad grew busier
Signed by President Millard Fillmore on September 18, 1850
Accused people got no jury trial and could not testify for themselves
Federal commissioners got $10 for sending an accused person south but only $5 for setting the person free
Helping a freedom seeker could bring a $1,000 fine and six months in jail; marshals could order bystanders to help
Helped inspire Harriet Beecher Stowe to write _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_ (1852)
Northern states passed “personal liberty laws” to block it
Anthony Burns (1854): federal troops marched him through Boston to a ship back to slavery in Virginia
Shadrach Minkins (1851): rescued from a Boston courtroom and taken to Canada
Daniel Webster backed it in his Seventh of March speech (1850)
After it passed, Harriet Tubman led freedom seekers all the way to St. Catharines, Canada
Written by Senator James Mason of Virginia
Came after _Prigg v. Pennsylvania_ (1842) ruled that state officials did not have to help capture freedom seekers
Strengthened a weaker 1793 law, signed by George Washington, that carried out a clause in Article IV of the Constitution
_Ableman v. Booth_ (1859): the Supreme Court said Wisconsin could not overrule it; Sherman Booth had helped free Joshua Glover
Jerry Rescue (1851): abolitionists in Syracuse, New York, freed William “Jerry” Henry
William and Ellen Craft fled from Boston to England when slave catchers came for them (1850)
Emerson called it a “filthy enactment”; Thoreau attacked it in the speech “Slavery in Massachusetts” (1854)
Whittier’s poem “Ichabod” attacked Webster for supporting it
John Brown formed the League of Gileadites in Springfield, Massachusetts (1851), to resist it
Harriet Tubman helped a crowd free Charles Nalle in Troy, New York (1860)
General Benjamin Butler called escaped men “contraband of war” (1861); Congress repealed it in June 1864
Thomas Sims (1851) was sent back from Boston to slavery in Georgia

trap.title: One law or the compromise?
trap.body: The Fugitive Slave Act was one of five laws in the Compromise of 1850, so the two answer lines share clues such as Henry Clay, Stephen Douglas, Daniel Webster, and Millard Fillmore. Saying “Compromise of 1850” when the question wants this one law is wrong, and so is the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which repealed the Missouri Compromise line and led to “Bleeding Kansas.” An older Fugitive Slave Act, signed by George Washington, dates from 1793.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this law” and mentions commissioners’ fees, jury trials, Shadrach Minkins, Anthony Burns, or personal liberty laws, say “Fugitive Slave Act.” If it asks for “this set of laws” or “this compromise” and mentions California’s statehood or the slave trade in Washington, D.C., say “Compromise of 1850.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 (accept Fugitive Slave Law; do not accept “Compromise of 1850” or “Kansas–Nebraska Act”)

topics.name: George Armstrong Custer
topics.kicker: Union cavalry general · Killed at the Battle of the Little Bighorn
topics.briefing: George Armstrong Custer finished last in his West Point class, then became a Union general at just 23, famous for his long golden hair and daring cavalry charges. After the Civil War he led the 7th Cavalry on the Great Plains. On June 25, 1876, he attacked a huge camp of Lakota and Cheyenne people along Montana’s Little Bighorn River, and warriors led by Crazy Horse and others defeated his troops; he and every soldier in his part of the regiment were killed.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man graduated last in his West Point class of 1861, but two years later, at only 23, he was promoted to brigadier general, making him one of the youngest generals in the Union army.
tossups.r: Newspapers called him the “Boy General.” For 10 points, name this cavalry officer who was killed at the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: On the last day of the Battle of Gettysburg, this man’s Michigan cavalry brigade helped stop J. E. B. Stuart’s Confederate horsemen in a fight east of town. He led his men into battle with the cry “Come on, you Wolverines!”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union cavalry general who later died fighting the Lakota and Cheyenne in 1876.

tossups.p: General Philip Sheridan bought the small table on which Ulysses S. Grant wrote out the terms of Robert E. Lee’s surrender and gave it to this man’s wife, Elizabeth. This man’s cavalry had helped block Lee’s escape in the final days of the war.
tossups.r: He later led the 7th Cavalry. For 10 points, name this commander who died at the Little Bighorn in 1876.

tossups.p: In 1867, this officer was court-martialed for leaving his post without permission to visit his wife, and he was suspended from the Army for a year without pay. Philip Sheridan called him back early to lead a winter campaign on the southern Plains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lieutenant colonel of the 7th Cavalry who was killed at the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In November 1868, this man’s soldiers attacked a Cheyenne village on the Washita [“WOSH-ih-taw”] River in what is now Oklahoma, killing the peace-seeking chief Black Kettle and many other people. Black Kettle had survived the Sand Creek Massacre four years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this commander of the 7th Cavalry, who was defeated at the Little Bighorn eight years later.

tossups.p: In 1874, this man led an Army expedition into the Black Hills, land promised to the Lakota by the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie. Reports of gold from that trip set off a rush of miners onto the land.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this officer whose 7th Cavalry was defeated at the Little Bighorn two years later.

tossups.p: In 1876, this man angered President Ulysses S. Grant by testifying to Congress about corruption linked to Secretary of War William Belknap. Grant at first refused to let this man go on that summer’s campaign against the Lakota.
tossups.r: Grant relented, and this man led the 7th Cavalry into Montana. For 10 points, name this officer killed at the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: A horse named Comanche, ridden by Captain Myles Keogh [“KEE-oh”], was found badly hurt but alive after this man’s final battle and became a famous symbol of that fight. Comanche’s preserved body is displayed at the University of Kansas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this commander of the 7th Cavalry, who died at the Little Bighorn in 1876.

tossups.p: This man’s younger brother Tom, who had won two Medals of Honor during the Civil War, died alongside him in 1876. Another brother, Boston, a teenage nephew, and his brother-in-law James Calhoun were also killed in that battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 7th Cavalry commander who was defeated at the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: Before his final battle, this man split his regiment, sending Major Marcus Reno to attack one end of a huge village and Captain Frederick Benteen to scout the hills to the south. Most of the soldiers with Reno and Benteen survived on a hilltop.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this commander who was killed with every soldier in his own part of the 7th Cavalry at the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: Eight days before this man’s death, warriors led by Crazy Horse fought General George Crook’s column to a standstill at the Battle of the Rosebud in Montana Territory. Crook’s men pulled back to resupply and took no part in the fighting that followed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 7th Cavalry commander defeated by Lakota and Cheyenne warriors at the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: This man’s regiment adopted the Irish tune “Garryowen” as its marching song. His last message, written by his adjutant and carried by trumpeter John Martin, told Captain Frederick Benteen: “Come on. Big village. Be quick. Bring packs.”
tossups.r: He led the 7th Cavalry. For 10 points, name this commander killed with all the soldiers under his direct command at the Little Bighorn in 1876.

tossups.p: This man wrote the memoir _My Life on the Plains_, and after his death his widow, Elizabeth, spent decades defending his reputation in books such as _Boots and Saddles_. She also wrote _Tenting on the Plains_ and _Following the Guidon_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cavalry officer who died at the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In 1991, Congress renamed a national monument in Montana that had been named for this man. In 2003, an Indian Memorial was added there to honor the Native people who fought and died in the battle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this commander of the 7th Cavalry, whose “Last Stand” took place in June 1876.

tossups.p: Weeks before this man’s death, the Hunkpapa [“HUNK-pah-pah”] Lakota leader Sitting Bull had a vision at a Sun Dance of soldiers falling into his people’s camp. The Lakota and Cheyenne call the battle that followed the Battle of the Greasy Grass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this U.S. cavalry commander who was killed in that battle, the Little Bighorn.

clues.t: Killed on June 25, 1876, with all the soldiers under his direct command, at the Battle of the Little Bighorn (his “Last Stand”)
Commanded the U.S. 7th Cavalry on the Great Plains
Defeated by Lakota and Cheyenne warriors; Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse were their best-known leaders
Union cavalry general in the Civil War, nicknamed the “Boy General”
Graduated last in his West Point class of 1861
At Gettysburg (July 3, 1863), his Michigan brigade helped stop J. E. B. Stuart’s cavalry
His battle cry: “Come on, you Wolverines!”
Led the 1874 Black Hills Expedition, which found gold on land promised to the Lakota by the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie
His troops attacked Black Kettle’s Cheyenne village on the Washita River (1868)
Split his regiment, sending Major Marcus Reno and Captain Frederick Benteen in other directions; most of their men survived
His wife, Elizabeth (“Libbie”), defended his memory in books like _Boots and Saddles_
His cavalry helped block Lee’s retreat; Sheridan gave his wife the table on which Grant wrote the surrender terms
Promoted to brigadier general at 23, days before Gettysburg (June 1863)
Court-martialed in 1867 for leaving his post to visit his wife; suspended for a year without pay
Wrote the memoir _My Life on the Plains_ (1874)
Angered President Grant by testifying (1876) about corruption tied to Secretary of War William Belknap
His brothers Tom (two Medals of Honor) and Boston died with him, along with a nephew and his brother-in-law
Comanche, Captain Myles Keogh’s horse, survived the battle; it is preserved at the University of Kansas
Eight days earlier, Crazy Horse fought George Crook to a standstill at the Rosebud (June 17, 1876)
His regiment’s marching tune was the Irish song “Garryowen”
His last message, written by his adjutant and carried by trumpeter John Martin: “Benteen. Come on. Big village. Be quick. Bring packs.”
Sitting Bull’s Sun Dance vision showed soldiers falling into the camp
The Lakota and Cheyenne call the battle the Greasy Grass
The battlefield monument once named for him was renamed in 1991; an Indian Memorial was added in 2003
Reburied at West Point in 1877; Errol Flynn played him in _They Died with Their Boots On_ (1941)

trap.title: The man or the battle?
trap.body: Many tossups ask for the Battle of the Little Bighorn instead of the man, and they share clues such as Sitting Bull, Crazy Horse, Reno, Benteen, Comanche, and the Greasy Grass. If the question says “this battle,” answering with his name is wrong. The Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) involved his old regiment, the 7th Cavalry, but happened 14 years after he died.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man,” “this officer,” or “this commander” means Custer; “this battle” or “this fight” means the Little Bighorn. West Point, Gettysburg, the Wolverines, the Washita, and the Black Hills Expedition are clues about his career. Lakota leaders such as Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse are their own answer lines.

topics.name: George McClellan
topics.kicker: Union general nicknamed the “Young Napoleon” · Lost to Lincoln in 1864
topics.briefing: George McClellan was skilled at building an army: after the Union defeat at Bull Run in 1861, he turned thousands of raw recruits into the well-trained Army of the Potomac, and his soldiers loved him. But he was so cautious that Abraham Lincoln reportedly complained he had “the slows.” After McClellan failed to chase Robert E. Lee’s army following Antietam, Lincoln removed him, and in 1864 McClellan ran against Lincoln for president and lost.
topics.answerHtml: George B. McClellan (accept George Brinton McClellan; prompt on “Little Mac” or “Young Napoleon”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After observing the Crimean War as part of a U.S. Army commission, this man designed a saddle that the American cavalry used for decades. He left the Army in 1857 to work for the Illinois Central Railroad.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union general who commanded the Army of the Potomac at Antietam.

tossups.p: Small victories in western Virginia, such as the Battle of Rich Mountain, helped this man win command of Union forces around Washington after the First Battle of Bull Run. That November, he replaced the aging Winfield Scott as general-in-chief.
tossups.r: His soldiers called him “Little Mac.” For 10 points, name this Union general nicknamed the “Young Napoleon.”

tossups.p: Confederate general John Magruder fooled this man by marching the same troops back and forth near Yorktown, helping convince him to begin a month-long siege in 1862. This man had moved his army by boat to the Virginia Peninsula to attack Richmond from the east.
tossups.r: This general’s soldiers called him “Little Mac.” For 10 points, name this commander of the Army of the Potomac.

tossups.p: During this man’s campaign against Richmond, Confederate general Joseph Johnston was wounded at the Battle of Seven Pines, and Robert E. Lee took command of the army facing him. Lee then drove this man away from Richmond in the Seven Days Battles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union general who later fought Lee again at Antietam.

tossups.p: Detective Allan Pinkerton ran this general’s spy service and gave him reports that greatly overestimated the size of the Confederate army. Those reports made this general, who already moved slowly, even more cautious.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union general who was removed from command of the Army of the Potomac in November 1862.

tossups.p: Days before one battle, Union soldiers found a copy of Robert E. Lee’s plans, Special Order 191, wrapped around three cigars, and passed it to this general. Even with that “Lost Order,” this general moved slowly, giving Lee time to gather his scattered army.
tossups.r: He then fought Lee at Antietam. For 10 points, name this commander of the Army of the Potomac.

tossups.p: In one 1862 battle, this general kept thousands of soldiers in reserve, including Fitz John Porter’s corps. Afterward, he let Robert E. Lee’s army retreat across the Potomac River into Virginia without chasing it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union commander at the Battle of Antietam, whom Lincoln removed weeks later.

tossups.p: When this general complained that his cavalry horses were tired and had sore tongues, Abraham Lincoln asked by telegram what those horses had done since the army’s last battle “that fatigue anything.” Lincoln is also said to have complained that this general had “the slows.”
tossups.r: Lincoln removed him from command in November 1862. For 10 points, name this general.

tossups.p: Confederate cavalry leader J. E. B. Stuart twice led his horsemen in a complete circle around this general’s army, once during the Peninsula Campaign and again in October 1862. The second ride took Stuart as far north as Chambersburg, Pennsylvania.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union general who commanded the Army of the Potomac in 1862.

tossups.p: In his Harrison’s Landing letter of July 1862, this general advised Abraham Lincoln not to turn the war into a fight to end slavery. Months earlier, he had gone to bed rather than meet Lincoln, who had been waiting at his house.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Union general who later ran against Lincoln for president.

tossups.p: This man ran for president with George Pendleton of Ohio on a platform that called the war a failure, but he rejected that “peace plank” in his letter accepting the nomination. He won only Kentucky, Delaware, and New Jersey.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Democrat who lost the 1864 election to Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: This man served as governor of New Jersey from 1878 to 1881, and his son of the same name later served as mayor of New York City. Earlier, the fall of Atlanta in September 1864 hurt this man’s chances of winning the presidency.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this former Union general who lost to Abraham Lincoln in 1864.

tossups.p: This man finished second in his West Point class of 1846 and served as an engineer under Winfield Scott in the Mexican-American War. In the 1850s, he helped survey possible routes for a railroad to the Pacific.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this general who led the Union’s Army of the Potomac in 1861 and 1862.

tossups.p: This general was criticized for slowly sending help to John Pope before the Second Battle of Bull Run in 1862. After Pope’s defeat, Abraham Lincoln put this general back in charge of the armies around Washington.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this general who weeks later fought Robert E. Lee at Antietam.

tossups.p: This general turned the beaten army from First Bull Run into a well-drilled force, and his soldiers deeply loved him. His replacement, Ambrose Burnside, lost at Fredericksburg about five weeks after taking command.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first commander of the Army of the Potomac, nicknamed “Little Mac,” whom Lincoln removed in November 1862.

clues.t: Organized and commanded the Union’s Army of the Potomac early in the Civil War
Fought Robert E. Lee at Antietam (September 17, 1862)
Democratic nominee who lost the 1864 election to Abraham Lincoln
Lincoln removed him in November 1862 for being too slow and cautious
Nicknamed the “Young Napoleon” and, by his soldiers, “Little Mac”
Peninsula Campaign (1862): moved his army by boat toward Richmond, but Lee drove him back in the Seven Days Battles
Replaced Winfield Scott as general-in-chief of the Union armies (November 1861)
Lincoln reportedly complained that he had “the slows”
Received Lee’s “Lost Order” (Special Order 191) before Antietam but still moved slowly
At Antietam, held back thousands of reserve troops and let Lee retreat into Virginia
Replaced by Ambrose Burnside, who then lost at Fredericksburg (December 1862)
Governor of New Jersey (1878–1881)
1864 running mate: George Pendleton; he rejected his party’s “peace plank,” which called the war a failure
Designed a cavalry saddle, named for him, after observing the Crimean War
Left the Army in 1857 to work for the Illinois Central Railroad
Second in his West Point class (1846); an engineer in the Mexican-American War
Detective Allan Pinkerton’s spies greatly overestimated Confederate numbers for him
John Magruder fooled him at Yorktown (1862) by marching troops back and forth
Joseph Johnston was wounded at Seven Pines (1862), so Robert E. Lee took command of the army facing him
Harrison’s Landing letter (July 1862): advised Lincoln not to make the war a fight to end slavery
J. E. B. Stuart rode completely around his army twice in 1862
Lincoln’s telegram asked what his horses had done since Antietam “that fatigue anything”
Went to bed rather than meet Lincoln, who was waiting at his house (November 1861)
Won only Kentucky, Delaware, and New Jersey in the 1864 election
Won small victories in western Virginia, such as Rich Mountain (1861), before taking command in Washington
His son of the same name was mayor of New York City (1904–1909)
Was slow to send help to John Pope before Second Bull Run (1862)

trap.title: Which Union general?
trap.body: Abraham Lincoln went through several top generals in the East, and their clues blur together. Irvin McDowell lost at First Bull Run; McClellan led the Peninsula Campaign and fought at Antietam; John Pope lost at Second Bull Run; Ambrose Burnside lost at Fredericksburg; Joseph Hooker lost at Chancellorsville; and George Meade won at Gettysburg.
trap.fix: “The slows,” the Peninsula Campaign, Pinkerton, the Lost Order, Antietam, and the 1864 Democratic nomination mean McClellan. Fredericksburg means Burnside, Chancellorsville means Hooker, and Gettysburg means Meade. His son, George B. McClellan Jr., a mayor of New York City, is a different person.
trap.line: Real answer line: George B. McClellan (accept George Brinton McClellan; prompt on “Little Mac” or “Young Napoleon”)

topics.name: George Wallace
topics.kicker: Alabama governor who fought desegregation · Ran for president four times
topics.briefing: George Wallace became governor of Alabama in 1963 vowing to defend segregation, and that June he stood in a doorway at the University of Alabama to block two Black students until federalized National Guard troops arrived. He ran for president four times, and in 1972 a gunman shot him in Maryland, leaving him paralyzed. In his later years, he said he had been wrong about segregation and asked for forgiveness.
topics.answerHtml: George Wallace (accept George Corley Wallace Jr.; do not accept “Lurleen Wallace”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man won a state Golden Gloves boxing championship. After earning a law degree from the University of Alabama in 1942, he served as a flight engineer on B-29 bombers in the Pacific during World War II.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who ran for president as a third-party candidate in 1968.

tossups.p: In June 1963, Deputy Attorney General Nicholas Katzenbach [“KATS-en-bahk”] confronted this man outside Foster Auditorium in Tuscaloosa, where he was trying to keep two Black students, Vivian Malone and James Hood, from enrolling.
tossups.r: President John F. Kennedy then federalized the Alabama National Guard. For 10 points, name this governor known for the “Stand in the Schoolhouse Door.”

tossups.p: Because Alabama’s constitution did not let him serve two terms in a row, this man’s wife, Lurleen, ran for governor in 1966 and won. She died in office in 1968, the same year this man ran for president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who ran as the American Independent Party candidate in 1968.

tossups.p: In 1968, this man won five Southern states and 46 electoral votes as a third-party candidate, with retired Air Force general Curtis LeMay as his running mate. His campaign slogan was “Stand Up for America.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who ran for president as the American Independent Party candidate.

tossups.p: Arthur Bremer was convicted of shooting this man at a shopping center in May 1972. The day after that attack, this man won the Democratic presidential primaries in Maryland and Michigan.
tossups.r: The shooting, in Laurel, Maryland, left him paralyzed. For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who made the “Stand in the Schoolhouse Door.”

tossups.p: In March 1965, this governor ordered Alabama state troopers to stop a voting rights march from Selma to Montgomery, and the troopers attacked the marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge on “Bloody Sunday.” Later that month, the march went ahead under federal protection.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor, who had made the “Stand in the Schoolhouse Door” two years earlier.

tossups.p: Federal judge Frank Johnson, who had been in law school with this man at the University of Alabama, ruled in a 1965 case bearing this man’s name that the Selma-to-Montgomery march could go forward.
tossups.r: The march ended at the state capitol in Montgomery. For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who had tried to stop it.

tossups.p: During one presidential campaign, this man claimed there was not “a dime’s worth of difference” between the Democratic and Republican parties. In that 1968 race, he carried his home state and four other Southern states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who ran on the American Independent Party ticket.

tossups.p: This former state circuit judge lost the 1958 race for governor of Alabama to John Patterson. After that defeat, he took a hard-line stand for segregation and won the governorship four years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who became Alabama’s governor in January 1963 and later ran for president four times.

tossups.p: On the evening of June 11, 1963, hours after this man ended a standoff with federal officials, President John F. Kennedy gave a televised speech calling for a new civil rights law. That law, the Civil Rights Act, was signed the next year by Lyndon Johnson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this governor who had tried to block two Black students from enrolling at the University of Alabama.

tossups.p: In 1964, this man made his first run for president, winning close to a third of the vote in the Democratic primaries in Wisconsin and Indiana and even more in Maryland. Those results showed that his message had support outside the South.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who later ran for president in 1968, 1972, and 1976.

tossups.p: In his later years, this man said he had been wrong about segregation and asked Black Alabamians for forgiveness. In 1982, he won his fourth and last term as governor with substantial support from Black voters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who had made the “Stand in the Schoolhouse Door” in 1963.

tossups.p: This man made his fourth and final run for president in 1976, when former Georgia governor Jimmy Carter defeated him in the Florida Democratic primary. By then, he had been using a wheelchair for four years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama governor who was shot in Laurel, Maryland, in 1972.

tossups.p: In January 1963, this man gave his first inaugural address as governor at the state capitol in Montgomery, standing on a star that marked the spot where Jefferson Davis had been sworn in as Confederate president.
tossups.r: In that speech, he vowed to defend segregation. That June, he made the “Stand in the Schoolhouse Door.” For 10 points, name this Alabama governor.

tossups.p: Brigadier General Henry Graham of the Alabama National Guard asked this man to step aside after President Kennedy placed the Guard under federal control. This man then left the doorway he had been blocking at Foster Auditorium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this governor who made the “Stand in the Schoolhouse Door” at the University of Alabama in 1963.

trap.title: Which segregationist governor?
trap.body: Several Southern governors tried to block school integration, and their clues get mixed up. George Wallace stood in the doorway at the University of Alabama in 1963; Orval Faubus of Arkansas used the National Guard to keep the Little Rock Nine out of Central High School in 1957; and Ross Barnett of Mississippi tried to stop James Meredith from entering the University of Mississippi in 1962. Strom Thurmond ran as a third-party Dixiecrat in 1948, twenty years before Wallace’s third-party run.
trap.fix: Alabama, Tuscaloosa, Vivian Malone and James Hood, Selma, the American Independent Party, and Laurel, Maryland, mean Wallace. Little Rock means Faubus, and Ole Miss means Barnett. Don’t confuse him with his wife, Lurleen Wallace, who was governor from 1967 to 1968, or with Henry Wallace, Franklin Roosevelt’s vice president.
trap.line: Real answer line: George Wallace (accept George Corley Wallace Jr.; do not accept “Lurleen Wallace”)

topics.name: Harry Reid
topics.kicker: Senate Majority Leader (2007–2015) · Nevada Democrat from Searchlight
topics.briefing: Harry Reid grew up in Searchlight, a tiny Nevada mining town, boxed as an amateur, and worked as a U.S. Capitol Police officer to help pay for law school. He represented Nevada in the U.S. Senate from 1987 to 2017 and was Senate Majority Leader from 2007 to 2015. In 2013 he led the “nuclear option” rules change for nominations, and in 2021, shortly before his death, Las Vegas’s main airport was renamed Harry Reid International Airport.

trap.body: Several modern Senate leaders show up in quiz bowl, and their clues blur together. topics.name: Haymarket Affair
topics.kicker: Bombing at an 1886 Chicago labor rally · Remembered every May Day
topics.briefing: Much of the world honors workers every May 1 because of what happened in Chicago in 1886. On May 4, as police moved in to break up a rally in Haymarket Square for an eight-hour workday, someone threw a bomb. Seven police officers and at least four other people died in the explosion and the gunfire that followed. Eight anarchists were convicted and four were executed, though no one ever proved who threw the bomb.
topics.answerHtml: Haymarket Affair (or Haymarket Square Riot or Haymarket Massacre; do not accept “Pullman Strike” or “Homestead Strike”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1893, Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned Samuel Fielden, Michael Schwab, and Oscar Neebe, three men who had been in prison since this event, declaring that their trial had been unfair. The pardons badly damaged Altgeld’s popularity.
tossups.r: Four other men had been executed for this event in 1887. For 10 points, name this 1886 bombing at a Chicago labor rally.

tossups.p: Mayor Carter Harrison listened to the speeches at the rally that ended in this event, decided the crowd was peaceful, and went home. Soon afterward, Samuel Fielden was finishing the last speech when police marched in and ordered the crowd to break up.
tossups.r: Moments later, a bomb exploded among the officers. For 10 points, name this violent end to a Chicago labor rally on May 4, 1886.

tossups.p: August Spies, one of the speakers at the rally that ended in this event, edited the German-language newspaper _Arbeiter-Zeitung_ [“AR-by-ter TSY-toong”]. The day before this event, Spies had watched police fire on strikers outside the McCormick reaper factory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 Chicago incident in which a bomb was thrown at police, after which Spies and three other anarchists were executed.

tossups.p: A labor federation that later became the American Federation of Labor had set May 1, 1886, as the date by which a shorter workday should become standard, and strikes spread across the country that week. Two days later, police shot strikers at a Chicago reaper factory.
tossups.r: The next night, a bomb exploded among police at a protest rally. For 10 points, name this 1886 Chicago event, which is remembered every May Day.

tossups.p: In 1889, socialist parties meeting in Paris formed the Second International and called for workers’ demonstrations around the world on the anniversary of the nationwide strikes that came just before this event. Those demonstrations grew into a yearly holiday in many countries.
tossups.r: That holiday is May Day, or International Workers’ Day. For 10 points, name this 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at police in Chicago.

tossups.p: Public fear after this event badly hurt the Knights of Labor, even though its leader, Terence Powderly, had condemned the radicals involved. Many workers turned instead to Samuel Gompers’s American Federation of Labor, founded later that same year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1886 Chicago incident in which someone threw a bomb at police officers breaking up a labor rally.

tossups.p: Albert Parsons, a Confederate army veteran who edited the anarchist newspaper _The Alarm_, fled Chicago after this event but walked into court on the first day of the trial to stand beside his fellow defendants. His wife, Lucy, later helped found the Industrial Workers of the World.
tossups.r: Parsons was one of four men executed in 1887 after this event. For 10 points, name this 1886 bombing at a Chicago labor rally.

tossups.p: Judge Joseph Gary refused to give separate trials to the eight men charged after this event, and he allowed jurors who admitted they were already prejudiced against the defendants. Seven of the eight men were sentenced to death.
tossups.r: Four of them were executed in 1887. For 10 points, name this 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at Chicago police during a rally for the eight-hour day.

tossups.p: Emma Goldman, who said this event inspired her to become an anarchist, is buried in Forest Park, Illinois, near a monument to the men convicted after it. Lucy Parsons, whose husband Albert was one of those men, is buried nearby.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 event in which a bomb exploded among Chicago police at a rally for the eight-hour workday.

tossups.p: In 1889, a statue of a police officer was put up near the site of this event to honor the officers who died there. Officer Mathias Degan was the first of those seven officers to die.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this May 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at police breaking up a Chicago labor rally.

tossups.p: Governor Richard Oglesby changed the death sentences of Samuel Fielden and Michael Schwab to life in prison the day before four other men were executed for this event. A fifth man sentenced to death, Louis Lingg, had died in his jail cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 incident in which a bomb was thrown at Chicago police during a labor rally in a public square.

tossups.p: Flyers printed in both English and German called workers to the meeting that ended in this event, held in a square on Randolph Street on a Tuesday evening. Much of the crowd had already gone home by the time police arrived.
tossups.r: During the last speech, police marched in, and someone threw a bomb. For 10 points, name this 1886 event in Chicago.

tossups.p: Oscar Neebe was sentenced to 15 years in prison while his seven co-defendants were sentenced to death in the trial after this event. Prosecutor Julius Grinnell never showed that any of the eight had thrown the bomb, arguing instead that their speeches and newspapers had encouraged the unknown bomber.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 incident at a Chicago labor rally that led to the execution of four anarchists.

tossups.p: Inspector John Bonfield led the column of police that marched in to break up the meeting that ended in this event. Seven officers and at least four other people died, many of them in the gunfire that followed an explosion, and the person who caused that explosion was never identified.
tossups.r: The meeting had been called to support the eight-hour workday. For 10 points, name this May 4, 1886, event in Chicago.

tossups.p: Speakers at the meeting that ended in this event stood on a wagon on Desplaines Street, and a sculpture of a speakers’ wagon was dedicated at that spot in 2004. August Spies, Albert Parsons, and Samuel Fielden all spoke that night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1886 Chicago incident in which a bomb was thrown at police, an event remembered each May Day.

trap.title: Haymarket, Homestead, or Pullman?
trap.body: Three famous Gilded Age labor clashes get mixed up. The Haymarket Affair (1886, Chicago) began when a bomb was thrown at police during a rally for the eight-hour day; the Homestead Strike (1892, Pennsylvania) was a fight at one of Andrew Carnegie’s steel mills; and the Pullman Strike (1894) was a nationwide railroad boycott led by Eugene Debs. Governor John Peter Altgeld shows up in both Haymarket and Pullman questions, because he pardoned the Haymarket prisoners and later protested federal troops during the Pullman Strike.
trap.fix: Anarchists, a bomb, May Day, and August Spies mean Haymarket. Carnegie, Henry Clay Frick, and Pinkerton guards mean Homestead. Debs, sleeping cars, and Grover Cleveland’s troops mean Pullman. If Altgeld comes up, wait for the year: 1886 is Haymarket, 1894 is Pullman.
trap.line: Real answer line: Haymarket Affair (or Haymarket Square Riot or Haymarket Massacre; do not accept “Pullman Strike” or “Homestead Strike”)

topics.name: Helen Keller
topics.kicker: Author and activist who was deafblind · Learned language from Anne Sullivan
topics.briefing: When she was 19 months old, an illness left Helen Keller unable to see or hear. At age 6, her new teacher, Anne Sullivan, began spelling words into her hand, and at a water pump in Tuscumbia, Alabama, Helen suddenly understood that “w-a-t-e-r” meant the cool liquid pouring over her other hand. She went on to graduate from Radcliffe College, write books, and travel the world speaking up for people with disabilities.
topics.answerHtml: Helen Keller (or Helen Adams Keller; do not accept “Anne Sullivan”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This person’s mother read about Laura Bridgman’s education at Boston’s Perkins Institution in Charles Dickens’s travel book _American Notes_. A Baltimore eye doctor then sent the family to Alexander Graham Bell, who told them to write to the Perkins school.
tossups.r: Perkins sent Anne Sullivan to be her teacher. For 10 points, name this woman from Alabama who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: In 1890, Sarah Fuller of Boston’s Horace Mann School for the Deaf began teaching this person to speak by letting her feel the position of Fuller’s tongue and lips. This person also learned to understand speech by touching a speaker’s lips and throat.
tossups.r: Her first teacher, Anne Sullivan, had taught her words by spelling them into her hand. For 10 points, name this author who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: Mark Twain persuaded the oil executive Henry H. Rogers and his wife to pay for this person’s college education. In 1904, she graduated with honors from Radcliffe College, where she had written her autobiography, _The Story of My Life_.
tossups.r: She was the first person who was deaf and blind to earn a bachelor’s degree. For 10 points, name this student of Anne Sullivan.

tossups.p: Patty Duke won an Academy Award for playing this person, and Anne Bancroft won one for playing her teacher, in a 1962 film based on William Gibson’s play. Both actresses had played the same roles on Broadway.
tossups.r: In that film’s most famous scene, this girl finally understands the word “water.” For 10 points, name this woman whose childhood is shown in _The Miracle Worker_.

tossups.p: Michael Anagnos, the director of a Boston school for the blind, chose one of its recent graduates, a young woman with poor eyesight of her own, to travel to Alabama and teach this girl. That teacher arrived on March 3, 1887.
tossups.r: That teacher, Anne Sullivan, worked with her for nearly 50 years. For 10 points, name this woman who lost her sight and hearing as a baby.

tossups.p: In 2009, Alabama added a bronze statue of this person as a young girl to the National Statuary Hall Collection in the U.S. Capitol. Six years earlier, Alabama put her on its state quarter, the first U.S. circulating coin with writing in Braille.
tossups.r: The statue shows her at the water pump where she first understood a word. For 10 points, name this woman who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: During a 1937 visit to Japan, this person was given an Akita puppy, often called the first Akita brought to the United States. She had been born in 1880 in Tuscumbia, Alabama.
tossups.r: An illness at 19 months had left her unable to see or hear. For 10 points, name this author whose teacher was Anne Sullivan.

tossups.p: This author dedicated her first book to Alexander Graham Bell, and a Harvard instructor named John Macy helped her edit it while she was still a college student. Macy married her teacher in 1905.
tossups.r: That 1903 book is _The Story of My Life_. For 10 points, name this woman who lost her sight and hearing as a baby.

tossups.p: This person joined the Socialist Party in 1909 and spoke out for women’s right to vote and for workers’ rights. In 1920, she was one of the founders of the American Civil Liberties Union.
tossups.r: She is best known for learning to communicate after losing her sight and hearing. For 10 points, name this activist from Tuscumbia, Alabama.

tossups.p: After this person’s teacher died in 1936, Polly Thomson, a Scottish woman who had worked with them since 1914, became her constant companion. This person died in 1968 at her home in Easton, Connecticut.
tossups.r: Her ashes were placed in Washington National Cathedral next to those of Anne Sullivan. For 10 points, name this author who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: This person worked for the American Foundation for the Blind for more than 40 years, raising money and speaking around the world. In 1964, Lyndon Johnson awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
tossups.r: As a child, she understood her first word, “water,” while standing at a pump. For 10 points, name this student of Anne Sullivan.

tossups.p: This person played herself in _Deliverance_, a 1919 silent film about her life. In the 1920s, she and her teacher toured the vaudeville stage, where she answered questions from the audience.
tossups.r: Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, had arrived at her Alabama home in 1887. For 10 points, name this woman who was deaf and blind.

tossups.p: This author described how she sensed the world through touch and smell in the 1908 book _The World I Live In_. Nearly fifty years later, she published a biography called _Teacher_.
tossups.r: That book honored Anne Sullivan, who taught her to communicate after she lost her sight and hearing. For 10 points, name this author.

tossups.p: For decades, the town where this person was born has held a summer festival in her honor, and a play about her childhood has been performed outdoors at her birthplace, Ivy Green. Her father, Arthur, had been a captain in the Confederate army.
tossups.r: That play is _The Miracle Worker_. For 10 points, name this woman from Tuscumbia, Alabama, who lost her sight and hearing as a baby.

tossups.p: This author explained her faith in the ideas of the Swedish thinker Emanuel Swedenborg in her 1927 book _My Religion_. She also wrote essays supporting workers and socialism, collected in _Out of the Dark_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this author who lost her sight and hearing as a baby and learned to communicate with help from Anne Sullivan.

trap.title: Student or teacher?
trap.body: Anne Sullivan, the teacher who spelled “water” into Keller’s hand, is an answer line of her own, and many clues (the Perkins school, the water pump, _The Miracle Worker_) show up in tossups about both women. The title _The Miracle Worker_ actually describes Sullivan, not Keller. Laura Bridgman, who was also deaf and blind and was educated at Perkins about fifty years earlier, can also be a tempting wrong answer.
trap.fix: If the question asks for the person who lost her sight and hearing at 19 months, graduated from Radcliffe, or wrote _The Story of My Life_, say Keller. If it asks for the Perkins graduate who arrived in Alabama in 1887 to teach, say Anne Sullivan.
trap.line: Real answer line: Helen Keller (or Helen Adams Keller; do not accept “Anne Sullivan”)

topics.name: Henry Ford
topics.kicker: Carmaker who built the Model T · Made the moving assembly line famous
topics.briefing: Henry Ford didn’t invent the car, but he figured out how to make cars cheap enough for ordinary families to buy. His Model T, introduced in 1908, was soon built on a moving assembly line that cut the time to put together a car’s chassis from more than 12 hours to about an hour and a half. In 1914, he shocked the business world by roughly doubling his workers’ pay to $5 a day, and by 1927 his company had built about 15 million Model Ts.
topics.answerHtml: Henry Ford (prompt on Ford; do not accept “Gerald Ford” or “Ford Motor Company”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In Aldous Huxley’s novel _Brave New World_, people use this man’s name in place of God’s and count the years from the debut of his most famous product. Huxley’s characters even make the sign of a letter of the alphabet in his honor.
tossups.r: That letter, T, stands for his most famous car. For 10 points, name this carmaker who introduced the moving assembly line.

tossups.p: In 1915, this man chartered the ocean liner _Oscar II_ and sailed to Europe with a group of peace activists, hoping to end World War I by Christmas. Newspapers mocked the voyage, which became known as the “Peace Ship.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this industrialist whose low-priced Model T put millions of Americans behind the wheel.

tossups.p: With Woodrow Wilson’s encouragement, this man ran for the U.S. Senate from Michigan in 1918 as a Democrat and narrowly lost to Truman Newberry. He also bought the weekly newspaper the _Dearborn Independent_ and used it to publish antisemitic articles in the early 1920s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Michigan industrialist who introduced the $5 workday in 1914.

tossups.p: After this man quit his second car company in 1902, his backers reorganized it under Henry Leland and renamed it Cadillac. A year earlier, this man had won fame by beating Alexander Winton in a car race at Grosse Pointe, Michigan.
tossups.r: In 1903, he founded the company that later built the Model T. For 10 points, name this automaker.

tossups.p: This man refused to pay for a license under George Selden’s patent on gasoline-powered cars, and in 1911 a federal appeals court ruled in his favor. Racer Barney Oldfield drove this man’s early race car, the “999,” to speed records.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of a Detroit car company whose Model T first went on sale in 1908.

tossups.p: In a 1916 interview with the _Chicago Tribune_, this man declared that “history is more or less bunk.” Yet he later spent a fortune collecting historic buildings, including Thomas Edison’s laboratory and the Wright brothers’ bicycle shop, for an outdoor museum called Greenfield Village.
tossups.r: That museum stands in Dearborn, Michigan, near where he was born. For 10 points, name this carmaker who built the Model T.

tossups.p: This man said he got an idea from the overhead trolleys that Chicago meatpackers used to move sides of beef past workers. Using that idea, his Highland Park plant cut the time needed to put together a car’s chassis from more than 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
tossups.r: His factories then turned out Model Ts by the millions. For 10 points, name this industrialist who introduced the moving assembly line in 1913.

tossups.p: Inspectors from this man’s “Sociological Department” visited workers’ homes to check whether they lived the way he approved, which decided whether they received his full pay. In 1926, he gave his factory workers a five-day, 40-hour week.
tossups.r: That full pay was the $5 day he announced in 1914. For 10 points, name this founder of the company that built the Model T.

tossups.p: In the 1937 Battle of the Overpass, security men working for this man’s company beat Walter Reuther and other United Auto Workers organizers outside the River Rouge plant. His company did not sign a contract with the union until 1941.
tossups.r: His company had become famous for its moving assembly line. For 10 points, name this automaker who introduced the $5 workday.

tossups.p: In 1928, this man’s company began building a town in the Amazon rainforest of Brazil to grow rubber for tires, but the plantation failed. Closer to home, his River Rouge complex in Dearborn turned iron ore, coal, and other raw materials into finished cars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American industrialist who introduced the Model T in 1908.

tossups.p: On October 21, 1929, the 50th anniversary of Edison’s light bulb, this man hosted Thomas Edison and President Herbert Hoover at the dedication of his museum in Dearborn. Years earlier, Edison had encouraged this man’s car experiments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this carmaker, who built the Model T on a moving assembly line.

tossups.p: This man built his first car in a brick shed behind his Detroit home and had to knock out part of the wall to drive it out. That 1896 vehicle, which rolled on four bicycle wheels, was called the Quadricycle.
tossups.r: Twelve years later, he introduced the low-priced Model T. For 10 points, name this Michigan automaker.

tossups.p: The brothers John and Horace Dodge, early investors in this man’s company, sued him to force the company to pay larger dividends, and in 1919 the Michigan Supreme Court ruled in their favor. The Dodges had supplied engines and other parts for his first cars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this founder of the car company that sold the Model T.

tossups.p: This man and his son Edsel created a foundation in 1936 that grew into one of the world’s largest charities. After Edsel died in 1943, this man ran his company again until his grandson took over in 1945.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Michigan industrialist whose company built the Model T on a moving assembly line.

tossups.p: In 1927, after building about 15 million of one model, this man shut down his factories for months to retool for its replacement, called the Model A. He had long resisted changing the older car.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this automaker whose “Tin Lizzie,” or Model T, came in “any color… so long as it is black.”
